topic: Should Toronto add housing supply primarily through private-sector incentives (cutting development charges, accelerating approvals) or through a city-as-developer model on city-owned land?
pull_quote: Research on Auckland's 2016 upzoning finds permitting roughly doubled within five years, while research on Vienna's limited-profit and municipal stock finds new social rents averaging close to 30 percent below private rents. Both mechanisms produce measurable supply, on different timelines, with different incidence on who actually moves in.

who_benefits.intro: Each candidate's preferred mechanism redistributes who pays and who benefits over different time horizons. The empirical literature on impact-fee incidence and on limited-profit housing systems lets the two paths be compared on the same framework.

mechanisms.summary: Cutting development charges and accelerating approvals tends to benefit, in the near term, owners of developable land and current homebuyers in active submarkets. Empirical work on impact-fee incidence (Skaburskis and Qadeer, 1992; Skaburskis, 2003) finds the burden shifts forward to buyers in competitive markets and back to landowners in supply-constrained or hot markets, so the savings from a DC cut do not flow uniformly to renters. A 2021 IMFG paper (Found, 2021) cautions that DCs can also be neutral or positive for affordability if they fund the infrastructure that makes new supply possible, meaning a cut may simply shift cost from new buyers to existing taxpayers.

City-as-developer plus the Purpose-Built Rental Incentives stream is designed to deliver units at rents below private-market levels, with affordability requirements (at least 20 percent affordable for 40 to 99 years) attached to a defined share of stock. Comparative work on Vienna finds limited-profit and municipal rents averaging roughly 27 to 30 percent below private rents (Kadi, 2024; Housing Europe, 2023). U.S. evidence on rent-restricted construction (Diamond, McQuade, and Qian, 2019) cautions that any policy that lowers rents below market without offsetting new construction can reduce overall rental supply, so the gain depends on whether the public-led units are net additions rather than substitutions.

positions.summary: Bradford has stated he would draw on Toronto's DC reduction funds and has called for development charges to be dropped, framing the city's current rental plan as too dependent on other governments. He has also released an office-to-residential conversion proposal: as-of-right approvals for conversions that do not enlarge the building, paired with a 20 percent affordable requirement.

positions.summary: Chow's stated target is approximately 25,000 additional rental homes layered on top of the HousingTO 2020-2030 Action Plan target of 65,000 rent-controlled homes, delivered through a mix of the Purpose-Built Rental Incentives stream (Council vote 23 to 1, November 2024) and a Public Developer Delivery model launched on city-owned sites in 2024. In March 2026, Chow signed a tri-government agreement with Carney and Ford that cuts DCs by 50 percent for three years on eligible projects.

status_quo.summary: As of the 2024 to 2025 HousingTO progress report, Toronto Council had approved nearly 30,000 new rent-controlled homes, about 46 percent of its 10-year target. City-led and city-supported projects accounted for roughly 65 percent of all rental housing starts in Toronto between January and August 2025. On the private side, Toronto CMA per-capita homebuilding fell to its lowest level since 1996 in 2025, driven by a roughly 60 percent drop in condominium starts; rental apartment starts also fell about 8 percent year over year. Toronto DCs on a non-rental one-bedroom rose from $4,985 in 2009 to $52,676 by 2024.

comparables.name: Auckland
comparables.summary: The Auckland Unitary Plan upzoned approximately three quarters of residential land in 2016, roughly tripling permitted dwelling capacity. Greenaway-McGrevy and Phillips (2023) find upzoning roughly doubled the permitting rate within five years and produced an approximate 80 percent increase in cumulative permits over six years.
comparables.outcome: Roughly 80 percent cumulative permit increase over six years; rents grew about 29 percent versus 47 percent income growth from 2016 to 2023, with the rent-to-income ratio falling from 22.7 to 19.4 percent.

citations.label: Greenaway-McGrevy and Phillips, The impact of upzoning on housing construction in Auckland, Journal of Urban Economics, 136, 103555, 2023
Greenaway-McGrevy, Can Zoning Reform Reduce Housing Costs? Auckland EPC Working Paper WP016

comparables.caveats: New Zealand has different DC regimes, weaker tenant protection law, and a smaller share of land owned by major institutional developers than Toronto.

comparables.name: Vienna
comparables.summary: Roughly 21 percent of Vienna's housing stock is municipally owned and another 18 to 21 percent is held by limited-profit housing associations (LPHAs), with new LPHA rents averaging about 27 percent below private rents. The OECD reports Austria spends about 0.25 percent of GDP on social housing, third highest in the OECD.
comparables.outcome: New LPHA rents average about 27 percent below private rents; Vienna's combined social share is near 44 percent of the city stock, sustained over decades.

citations.label: Kadi, Layers of Commodification in the City of Decommodification, Housing, Theory and Society, 2024
OECD Housing Policy Toolkit, Austria snapshot, 2023

comparables.caveats: Austria has unitary federal-state housing law, decades of accumulated public land, and a non-profit institutional sector with no Canadian equivalent at scale.

comparables.name: Houston
comparables.summary: Houston cut minimum lot sizes from roughly 5,000 to 1,400 square feet inside Loop 610 in 1998, later citywide, catalyzing thousands of small-lot infill homes. Glaeser and Gyourko's regulatory-tax estimates place Houston's regulatory tax near zero, versus 20 percent or more in tightly regulated coastal markets.
comparables.outcome: Regulatory tax on housing measured near zero; thousands of small-lot infill homes built where minimum lot sizes were reduced.

citations.label: Glaeser and Gyourko, The Economic Implications of Housing Supply, Journal of Economic Perspectives, 32(1), 2018, DOI 10.1257/jep.32.1.3

comparables.caveats: Houston has no zoning code in the Toronto sense, a Sun Belt land-supply context, and weaker design and heritage protections than any Canadian city.

comparables.name: Berlin
comparables.summary: Berlin's Mietendeckel froze and rolled back rents from February 2020 until April 15, 2021, when the Federal Constitutional Court ruled it void on federalism grounds, retroactively obligating tenants to repay foregone rent. Pre-ruling research found short-run rent reductions in regulated stock and reduced supply on listing platforms.
comparables.outcome: Rent cap ruled void after 14 months; short-run rent reductions in regulated stock paired with reduced platform supply, then retroactive repayment of foregone rent.

citations.label: Bundesverfassungsgericht, Press release 28/2021, Act Governing the Rent Cap for Residential Premises in Berlin is void, April 15, 2021

comparables.caveats: Included as a cautionary case on the limits of rent control as a stand-alone supply lever, not as a model either Toronto candidate is proposing.

comparables.name: Singapore HDB
comparables.summary: Roughly 77 to 80 percent of Singapore's resident population lives in Housing and Development Board flats, with about 90 percent of HDB residents owning their unit, financed through Central Provident Fund withdrawals.
comparables.outcome: About 77 to 80 percent of residents housed in HDB flats; about 90 percent of HDB residents own their unit.

citations.label: Singapore Housing and Development Board, official statistics
Statista, Share of resident population in HDB flats, 2023

comparables.caveats: Singapore is a city-state with full control over land assembly, a compulsory savings system, and a unitary national government. Included only as the high-end of what state-as-developer can reach in principle, not as a proposal under either Toronto platform.

projections.rationale: Literature does not support a confident singular projection on this question. Toronto-specific evidence is thin: the city's own 2024 to 2025 progress data show 65 percent of recent rental starts came from city-led or city-supported channels under the current policy mix, but isolating the marginal effect of DC cuts versus public delivery requires a counterfactual the published research does not yet provide. The comparable-jurisdiction outcomes (Auckland's roughly 80 percent cumulative permit increase over six years; Vienna's new social rents averaging roughly 27 to 30 percent below private rents at sustained 0.25 percent of GDP public spend) are the closest defensible numerical anchors.

time_horizon: Auckland's permitting response showed up within one to three years; Vienna's stock share took roughly three decades of sustained public investment; Berlin's rent-cap experiment unwound in 14 months. For Toronto, the published evidence supports near-term effects (years 1 to 3) on permits from approval-speed and DC changes, and decade-scale effects on stock composition from city-as-developer programs.
